A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Gauss-Seidel projection method. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations on six biomolecular benchmarks, runtime and convergence measurements, qualitative predictions, and a finetuning/projection ablation.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark evaluations and adds empirical studies of projection stability, penalty sensitivity, denoising budgets, computational overhead, and structural perturbations.

M1.justification: The projection objective, Gauss-Seidel updates, implicit differentiation, and Algorithms 1–4 are retained. The Boltz-2 experiment applies the already-described post-processing capability without documenting a new algorithmic component or procedural adaptation.

E1.justification: Both versions use RCSB training data and evaluate CASP15, Test, PoseBusters, AF3-AB, dsDNA, and RNA-Protein. The added analyses use retained biomolecular tasks and datasets; different step budgets, solver parameters, and individual examples do not establish expanded task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds AlphaFold3 comparisons on CASP15, Test, and PoseBusters in Table 1. Figure 7 adds the Boltz-2-plus-GS variant, while Figure 5 now separately reports Protenix and Protenix-Mini runtimes. These materially extend the comparisons beyond v1's reported comparator configurations.

E3.justification: V2 adds TM-score, removes Mean LDDT-PLI reporting, and adds protein-protein interface scores for AF3-AB. It introduces ten-step Protenix-Mini evaluations, comparisons at 2/5/10/200 denoising steps, and a separate PXMeter docking evaluation. New profiling uses token-count bins on an A100. Section 4.1 also expands the reported penalty choice from 10^-7 to 10^-7 or 10^-6; this does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendices B–G examine projection repeatability, penalty sensitivity, accuracy and validity across step budgets, Boltz-2 post-processing, module runtime and memory, docking-tool dependence, and structural perturbations. These address distinct questions beyond v1's convergence comparison, qualitative examples, and finetuning ablation.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly specifies five independent projection runs per denoised PoseBusters structure and reports pairwise RMSD of 0.0000 ± 0.0000 Å. Both versions already report uncertainty using ± values; changed error magnitudes do not establish a different estimator or increased repetition of the main benchmarks.

E6.justification: Many benchmark and ablation values are revised, alongside substantial new result entries. For example, Table 1 changes Protenix's CASP15 Complex LDDT from 0.54 ± 0.04 to 0.65 ± 0.06. Section 5.4 changes the reported Protenix-Mini speedup from about 9.5× to 2.3×, assigning 9.5× to Protenix. New results include projection perturbation RMSD of 0.1865 ± 0.0219 Å and PXMeter scores. The PDFs do not explain the cause of every numerical revision.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, constraint definitions, and convergence proofs are retained; v1 Appendices D–G correspond to v2 Appendices I–L. The new uniqueness discussion restates the linearized-system uniqueness property already established in v1, while its repeated-projection evidence is empirical.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: differentiable projection during training and inference enables physically valid two-step predictions with competitive accuracy and approximately tenfold speedups over 200-step baselines. The additional evaluations do not redefine that contribution.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 narrows improvement over Protenix-Mini from all to most benchmarks, replaces outperformance language with comparability, and removes the ligand-interface leadership explanation. New appendices discuss penalty-dependent failure, projection stability and structural preservation, attribute the remaining Boltz-2 accuracy gap to the base model and training data, and explain docking-score discrepancies through evaluation tools.

D1.justification: V2 adds a ProteinGS repository address and states that code is available. It newly identifies OpenStructure as the primary docking evaluator and documents A100 hardware and CUDA kernels for the added profiling study. Existing training hardware, training duration, solver settings, and pseudocode are largely retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a paragraph positioning the method against diffusion finetuning approaches DRaFT, DPPO, DPOK, and DiffPPO. References to OpenStructure and Matrix Computations are also added. The existing positioning relative to biomolecular predictors, diffusion steering, and position-based dynamics remains.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition and the main section sequence are retained. V2 makes local grammar and terminology edits, updates the publication header and author formatting, adds a related-work paragraph, and reorganizes the appendices around the new analyses. This is not an extensive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain rows and metric columns, and Table 2 moves into the main text. V2 adds Figures 6–8 and Table 3, revises the runtime chart and its legend, and expands Figure 4's caption. The earlier qualitative and constraint figures remain as Figures 9–11 rather than being removed.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny through matched-budget comparisons, solver sensitivity tests, structural perturbation measurements, and isolated training overhead analysis, addressing important gaps in v1's practical validation. It also corrects the overstated Protenix-Mini speed comparison and moderates the accuracy discussion. These gains improve support and calibration of the central claims, although many revised benchmark values remain unexplained and the formal guarantees are unchanged.
